title: Up or Out
protagonist: Ilse Marchetti, first-year community-college student handling her grandparents' paperwork (fictional), with architect Tomas Quartey (fictional)
primary_metric: expected declared cost of the addition, in dollars, averaged over nine equally likely job sizes (250 to 450 sq ft in steps of 25), where cost at a size = median declared cost per sq ft of comparable signed-off NYC filings within +/-50 sq ft of that size x the size; lower wins. Margin = gap divided by the lower (winner's) value.

options.A: The Tall Plan: file a vertical enlargement, a partial new floor over the existing house
options.B: The Wide Plan: file a horizontal enlargement, an extension into the rear yard

scenario_constructions: Ilse Marchetti, Tomas Quartey, Nonna and the house are fictional. The savings, the architect's size range and the equal-likelihood rule are stated scenario assumptions (Appendix F). The filings are real and anonymous: no owner, applicant or address is pulled or shown.
sensitivity_note: Facilitator note (SPEC §6): family finances and housing for an aging relative; keep to numbers and the decision, do not ask students to disclose their home situation; if students browse the dataset, it contains real owners' names and addresses and they should not search for or post identifiable people. Nothing here is construction, permit or legal advice.

deliverables.text: Box plots at both ends of the range: side-by-side box-and-whisker plots of cost per square foot for each plan in the 250 sq ft window and the 450 sq ft window from raw values, with five-number summaries, outliers by the 1.5 x IQR rule, and a one-sentence overlap reading per window.

The size curve: scatter plot of median cost per square foot against job size for both plans, slope of each plan's curve over 250-300 and 350-450 sq ft, a linear versus non-linear call, and the interpolated job size at which the cheaper plan changes.
All sizes pooled: the all-sizes gap as a percent of the lower median, an explanation from the size mix of why it does not answer the family's question, and a comparison with the per-size gaps.

The cost memo: cost at each of nine sizes (median $/sq ft times sq ft) for each plan, the average over the nine, the gap in dollars and as a percent of the lower average, and the sizes at which each plan exceeds the savings.
The decision under an unknown size: each plan's largest regret over the nine sizes, and one fact from Appendix E to check before signing with the plan it favors.

balance.argument_a: The Tall Plan has the lower expected cost over the architect's range ($135,817 vs $140,206, 3.2%) and is cheaper at six of the nine sizes, by 17% to 36% from 325 sq ft up (saving about $21,000 to $45,000). The small-size cliff is probably a scope artifact: small Tall filings carry higher total declared costs and fewer added stories, so an addition-only job likely avoids it.
balance.argument_b: The Wide Plan has the smaller worst case (largest regret $44,927 vs $74,335) and a flat cost per sq ft ($364 to $437) across the range, with 2.5 to 3 times the evidence per window; it is cheaper by up to 70.5% at the small sizes, and the Tall cliff persists among filings that report added stories, so the scope-artifact argument is an inference, not a fact.
balance.margin_basis: Gap divided by the lower expected cost over nine sizes: (140,206 - 135,817) / 135,817 = 3.2%. The winner is not statistically distinguishable (bootstrap: Tall wins 52% of resamples).

context_glossary.desc: In New York City's zoning law, an addition to the floor area of an existing building. A vertical enlargement builds up; a horizontal enlargement builds out.
The city's category for a major alteration that changes a building's use, exits or occupancy. Every filing in this case's records is this type.
The open ground behind a house. The Wide Plan builds into it.
City rules on what can be built where and how big. This case does not model them.

context_why_notes.D1: Why box plots at the two ends: a median alone hides how spread out the costs are; the boxes show whether a gap between medians is bigger than the spread.
context_why_notes.D2: Why a size curve: cost per square foot changes with job size, so one number per plan cannot describe it.
context_why_notes.D3: Why compare the pooled gap with the per-size gaps: mixing sizes together can hide what happens at any one size.
context_why_notes.D4: Why average over sizes: nobody knows the size yet, so the fair comparison weighs every size the architect says is possible.
context_why_notes.D5: Why regret: two plans can cost the same on average and still differ in how bad their worst case is.
